## Simple explanation

Metadata is information about data. A photo's metadata might include when it
was taken; a dataset's metadata might describe its columns, source, and
collection date.

## Technical explanation

Metadata is descriptive or administrative information associated with a
dataset, model, experiment, or service. It can include schemas, provenance,
versions, ownership, timestamps, licensing, or configuration. Metadata is
distinct from the primary payload, though in practice it may be stored
alongside or embedded within it.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Metadata helps teams discover data, understand its limitations, reproduce
experiments, and track model lineage. Without reliable metadata, it is harder
to determine what a model was trained on, which artifact is deployed, or
whether a dataset is appropriate for a use case.

## How it works

Teams define metadata fields and record them at data ingestion, training,
evaluation, and deployment. Registries or catalogs can make those records
searchable. Metadata should be versioned and validated because missing or
incorrect descriptions can mislead downstream users.

## Practical example

A dataset catalog entry can record a dataset's owner, schema, source,
collection period, license, and known limitations so engineers can assess it
before training.

## Common misconceptions

- Metadata does not guarantee that the underlying data is accurate or appropriate.
- A filename alone is rarely enough metadata to reproduce an experiment.
- Metadata can itself contain sensitive information and may need access controls.
